newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to send Cuban refugees back home.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to send Cuban refugees back home.

text.p: Cuban refugees reaching the United States illegally will be sent back to Cuba from now on, U.S. immigration officials said on Monday.
The controversial move, discussed for several months, marks the end of a policy of virtually automatic asylum for Cubans and has angered Cuban exiles in the United States.
"This is this closing of the 'undergroud railway'," Miami Republican congressman Lincoln Diaz-Balart told Reuters. "It will be seen by history as an infamous step."

Lemar Wooley, an Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS) spokesman, said the Miami immigration office received the new instructions on Friday. They went into effect immediately, retroactive from Dec. 6.
The Cubans could only be returned if the Havana government accepted them, he added.

"Cuban migrants who illegally entered the United States after Dec. 6, 1996, are being treated as illegal entrants and are being placed into proceedings as are all illegal entrants from other countries," the INS said in a brief statement on Saturday.

Immigration officials declined to describe the move as a change in policy, but it caps a gradual shift in treatment of Cuban refugees. In May, Washington announced "rafters" picked up at sea would be returned to the communist-ruled island.
Thousands of people have risked their lives to flee Cuba over the years, crossing the Straits of Florida in flimsy boats, rafts and inflated inner tubes for tires.
Unlike illegal migrants from other countries, they were allowed to stay in the United States because of Washington's hostility to President Fidel Castro's government.
In September 1994, after a crisis in which 30,000 Cubans tried to cross the straits, Washington and Havana reached a pact under which the United States would issue 20,000 visas a year.
The new directive on illegal arrivals, reached after talks between U.S. and Cuban officials, was aimed in part at bolstering the legal migration accord, INS officials said.

The closing of the back door has infuriated the large Cuban community in Miami. Cuban exile groups earlier this month issued a joint statement calling it an "infamy" and demanding President Bill Clinton reverse the policy.
Diaz-Balart, who is of Cuban origin, said on Monday: "It needs to be condemned and the protests have to continue. This is totally unacceptable."

He said the Clinton administration wanted to normalise relations with Cuba. But it had been frustrated because of the tightening of a U.S. embargo on the island prompted by Cuba's shooting down in February of two planes of an exile group, Brothers to the Rescue.
"The refugees are bearing the brunt of that," he said.
Cubans now held in detention in Miami or elsewhere in the United States will be paroled if they arrived before Dec. 6 and provided they are not crimanals, the INS said.
The first three were released this weekend from the Krome Avenue Detention Centre in Miami.
There were 204 Cubans in Krome and other centres, of whom 124 allegedly committed criminal acts.
